title: Why Novices shouldn't do Box Squats
summary: NH argues that box squats are not an easier or better substitute for back squats for novices. The box gives you something to push off, a square box forces a sit-back, wide-stance, good-morning pattern, it skips the hardest part of the squat, and it does not build mobility. He suggests turning the box into a triangle and recommends box front squats as the one useful variant.
claims: Box squats are often given to novices as an easier intro to knee flexion; he believes that is wrong and they should not replace squats for novices or others
Difficulty depends on box height: a box above parallel is obviously easier, and even a box below parallel is easier than a free squat because you have something to push off
The glutes touching the box adds contact points, which makes the lift easier even if more technical, so carryover is not one-to-one
A square box set up behind you forces the shins forward and the hips back; in a free squat that becomes a good morning
Novices then widen their stance to clear the box, which is unnatural; very wide stances suit only big lifters with wide hips
A closer stance requires more knee flexion to reach parallel and so more quad tension; a wider stance shortens the range of motion and shifts work to the hips, posterior chain and lower back
The box reinforces the forward lean novices already have from poor thoracic extension
A box does not fix mobility because it stops you at the same depth every time; better to squat high and go deeper over months with submaximal weight, e.g. paused squats
The box allows more weight, so novices think they are getting stronger at the squat when they are only getting stronger at the box squat
Novices who box squat for months and then free squat usually cannot reach parallel and are weak
The box catches you exactly where the squat becomes hard: the hard part is out of the hole until the knee passes hip angle
Easy fix: turn the box so a corner points forward (a triangle), letting your legs go on each side without a super-wide stance
Sitting, rocking back to vertical and pushing up uses the momentum of the negative; it has no carryover and is like bouncing the bar off the chest
A proper box squat is straight down and up; pausing on the box defeats its purpose because you still push off it
Studies claiming box squats activate as much muscle used more weight on the box squat, so their design is flawed
Telling someone who good-mornings their squat to use a box is terrible advice; the box teaches the good morning
Fix the good morning with technique work, thoracic extension, strengthening the core and glutes, and paused squats with a 1-second pause at the bottom
Bodybuilders can use a box but get less than from normal squats, and most of their variations will be without one
The box front squat is the one version he likes: the front rack already enforces an upright torso, and the box helps with the front squat's real limiter, losing the rack

The back squat is mostly muscular with some technique, while the front squat is mostly technical; on the back squat you can still grind with bad form, on the front squat the set ends when the bar slips
He does and recommends box front squats at or below parallel, preferring parallel; he never programs box back squats, especially for novices
exercises: turn box into a triangle; straight down and up, no rocking; no pause
easier and reinforces sit-back good morning; poor carryover
1 s pause at bottom; can be done high and progressively deeper
builds mobility and fixes good-morning tendency
box at or below parallel, parallel preferred; reset on box
front rack keeps torso upright; box prevents losing the rack
more knee flexion and quad tension than wide stance
